titre: Nothing Is Dirty, Everything Is Out of Place
accroche: A shoe set on the table is not dirty because of germs. It is dirty because it is in the wrong place.
contenu_vulgarise:
Perfectly clean shoes, set on the dinner table. No one will touch anything until they have been taken off it. A table is for putting food on, not shoes. It is this banal intuition that the British anthropologist Mary Douglas takes seriously in Purity and Danger, published in 1966: dirt is not a property of objects. It is a matter of classification.

## A system, not a substance

Douglas, trained at Oxford under Evans-Pritchard, builds her demonstration on ethnographic comparisons, notably her own fieldwork among the Lele of the Belgian Congo. Her thesis: what a culture calls “dirty” is what escapes its categories, what blurs a boundary that its classification system holds to be clear-cut. One example she develops at length: the dietary prohibitions of Leviticus, chapter 11. The Hebrew text declares clean those land animals that chew the cud AND have a cloven hoof: the ox, the sheep. The pig has a cloven hoof but does not chew the cud; the camel chews the cud but does not have a cloven hoof. Neither is unclean in a hygienic sense: each meets only one of the two criteria that define the category, and thus blurs the boundary the text wants to keep sharp.

## A quotation that is also out of place

The formula that sums up the whole book, “dirt is matter out of place,” has become a commonplace of anthropology and well beyond. Douglas herself attributes it to Lord Chesterfield, an 18th-century British statesman. The problem: neither his own biographer, Richard Fardon, nor the historian Alan Macfarlane has ever found this sentence in a text by Chesterfield, despite dedicated searches. The closest formulation identified goes back to 1852, in a speech by Lord Palmerston, who said he had “heard it said that dirt is nothing but a thing in a wrong place,” proof that the expression was already circulating as a saying before him. Everything suggests that Douglas picked up a floating aphorism, condensed it into its most memorable form, and sourced it wrongly.

The irony has not escaped anyone: an entire book devoted to showing that nothing is dirty in itself, only badly classified, contains at its heart a quotation that is itself badly classified. Douglas, moreover, never stopped revisiting her own work: in Leviticus as Literature, published in 1999, she rejects most of her 1966 reading of Leviticus and substitutes a more complex explanation, centered on the architecture of the tabernacle rather than on animal anomaly alone. The book that taught a whole discipline to distrust overly neat classifications ended up revising its own.

citation.texte: If we can abstract pathogenicity and hygiene from our notion of dirt, we are left with the old definition of dirt as matter out of place.

carte.punch: The quotation that sums up the book is itself out of place.
carte.idee: Mary Douglas shows in 1966 that dirt is not a property of objects. It is an effect of classification. Irony: the quotation that sums up the book, attributed by Douglas to Lord Chesterfield, has never been found in his writings.

quiz.question: For Mary Douglas, why is the pig classified as unclean in Leviticus?
choix: Because it transmitted diseases identified by the priests of the time
Because raising it was reserved for the priests of the Temple
Because the text classes it among the sacred animals, reserved for sacrifice
It meets only one of the two criteria for clean animals, and blurs the category
quiz.explication: Leviticus defines clean land animals by two joint criteria, chewing the cud and having a cloven hoof. The pig meets only one: neither disease, nor priestly status, nor sacredness enters into Douglas's explanation, only classification.
